definition: Baseline for outputs that require review before use: (1) Factually correct? Are facts, figures, dates, and names accurate? (2) Complete? Are relevant aspects missing? (3) Appropriate? Does the tone fit, and does the wording contain discriminatory claims? Review depth and additional controls depend on purpose and impact.
A natural or legal person that develops an AI system, or has one developed, and places it on the market under its own name (EU AI Act Art. 3(3)).
A mechanism that computes weighted relationships between token representations. It helps transformer models connect contextual information; it does not establish relevance or understanding.
A contractual arrangement under GDPR Art. 28 when a controller engages a processor to process personal data. Whether a DPA is required and sufficient depends on the parties' roles and the processing.

Rights of natural persons under the GDPR: access (Art. 15), rectification (Art. 16), erasure (Art. 17), restriction of processing (Art. 18) and objection (Art. 21). These rights also apply when AI systems process personal data.
A natural or legal person, public authority, agency, or other body using an AI system under its authority; personal non-professional activity is excluded (EU AI Act Art. 3(4)).

A systematic deviation that can arise from data collection, labels, objectives, modeling, evaluation, or deployment context. It can affect groups differently but does not automatically constitute discrimination in every case.

A collection of relevant EU AI Act records: an AI inventory, risk classifications, training records, usage policies and incident-response protocols. It supports documentation but does not replace a legal review.
A field of AI concerned with processing and analysing images and video. Applications include facial recognition, quality control and autonomous driving.
An assessment under GDPR Art. 35 when planned processing is likely to result in a high risk to natural persons' rights and freedoms. AI can be a risk factor but does not automatically trigger a DPIA.
An example model that assigns company data to four protection levels. The organization defines the labels, criteria, and permitted workflows; the level alone does not approve a product.
A branch of machine learning that uses artificial neural networks with many layers. It enables pattern recognition in complex data such as images, speech and text.

AI-generated or manipulated image, audio, or video content resembling real people, objects, places, or events and capable of falsely appearing authentic. The legal definition depends on the applicable framework.
Additional training of a pretrained model on selected data or preferences to adjust behavior for particular tasks or domains. Success must be checked with separate evaluations.
AI systems that create new content such as text, images, audio, video and code. Examples include ChatGPT, DALL-E, Midjourney and Claude.
Plausible output from a generative model that is unsupported, inconsistent, or factually wrong. Language-model generation provides no automatic guarantee of fact checking.

An AI system classified as high-risk under Art. 6 in conjunction with Annex I or III. The obligations of providers and deployers differ. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force since 27 July 2026, sets 2 December 2027 for stand-alone Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for systems integrated into products.

A design in which people have defined monitoring, intervention, or decision authority. Article 14 of the EU AI Act requires effective human oversight for high-risk systems; a human final decision is not configured identically in every use case.
The process in which a trained model processes an input and produces an output. Every ChatGPT response is an inference.

Skills, knowledge, and understanding that enable informed AI use and awareness of opportunities, risks, and possible harm (EU AI Act Art. 3(56)). Article 4 requires context-specific measures supporting the development of this literacy.
A machine-based system that generates outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations or decisions from inputs and can operate with varying levels of autonomy (EU AI Act Art. 3(1)).

A procedure for assessing whether the requirements applicable to a high-risk AI system are met. The procedure and involvement of a notified body depend on the system and legal basis; CE marking follows only where the framework requires it.

A technical umbrella term for machine-based systems that derive outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions from inputs. The exact definition depends on the technical or legal context.

A large model for token sequences trained on extensive data to model probabilities over outputs. Depending on the model, it may process modalities beyond text; product names and model versions should be distinguished.

A field of AI in which model parameters are adjusted using data and optimization objectives. Supervised, unsupervised, self-supervised, and reinforcement learning are common, non-exhaustive categories.
The trained result of a machine-learning process. It contains the learned parameters, or weights, and can be applied to new inputs.
A field of AI concerned with processing natural language. Its applications include translation, summarisation, sentiment analysis and text generation.
A computational model inspired by biological neurons. It consists of layers of connected nodes and is the basis of deep learning.
A model fits peculiarities or noise in the training data too closely and therefore generalizes less well to new data. Memorization can be a symptom but is not the only form.
Values adjusted during training, including weights and bias terms. Parameter count alone does not provide a reliable comparison of quality, cost, or suitability.
Input to a generative system, including instructions, questions, data, and context. A clear prompt can influence output but does not determine correctness or quality by itself.

A versioned collection of prompt templates for recurring tasks, with purpose, permitted inputs, example outputs, review steps, and evaluation results. Benefits and limitations must be measured in the actual workflow.

An attack or failure mode in which instructions in user input or processed content influence a model outside the intended behavior. OWASP lists Prompt Injection as LLM01 in its 2025 Top 10 for LLM applications.

A pattern in which a generative model receives retrieved content as context. It can improve traceability and factual accuracy but depends on retrieval, source quality, and correct use and does not prevent hallucinations.
A course template with the fields Role, Context, Task, Format, and Constraints. It makes requirements visible; not every task needs every field, and the template does not guarantee correct output.

A type of machine learning in which an agent learns through trial and error. Desired behaviour receives rewards and undesired behaviour receives penalties. Applications include robotics and game strategies.
Use of AI services or features outside the approved inventory and intended controls. It can involve consumer services, extensions, embedded features, or local models.

A type of machine learning that uses labelled training data. The model learns mappings from inputs to outputs through examples. Applications include spam filtering, credit scoring and image recognition.
The smallest unit that an LLM processes. A token can be a word, part of a word or a punctuation mark. Models generate text one token at a time.
Data used to adjust model parameters. Selection, quality, representativeness, and documentation influence behavior; the model, objective, evaluation, and deployment context also matter.

A neural-network architecture introduced in 2017 that uses attention and positional information. It underpins many current language models and enables highly parallel training; modern models do not all use an identical architecture.

A type of machine learning that uses unlabelled data. The model identifies patterns and structures without labelled examples. Applications include customer segmentation, anomaly detection and clustering.
